destinations.name: Washington
facts: The Washington Monument is 169 metres tall. A law from 1910 keeps every other building in the city lower, so it still rules the skyline.
The famous cherry trees along the Tidal Basin were a gift from the city of Tokyo, in 1912.
The city was designed from scratch: Pierre L'Enfant drew its streets and avenues in 1791.

greeting.meaning: Twelve stops, one big circle around the world. Your passport is almost full.

facts: The journey ends where it began

steps.title: Retrace the route
steps.blurb: Tap the stops in the order you visited them.
steps.intro: Watch the stops light up on the map, then tap them back in the same order. Each round adds one more place. If you get lost, the game shows you the sequence again.
steps.fact: In December 2011, Samoa moved to the west side of the International Date Line and skipped a whole day: December 30 never happened there.

steps.title: Cherry blossoms
steps.blurb: Catch the falling blossoms at the Tidal Basin.
steps.intro: Back in Washington, the cherry trees around the Tidal Basin burst into bloom every spring. Drag left and right to catch the petals, and let the raindrops fall.
steps.fact: The first cherry trees were a gift from the city of Tokyo in 1912: about 3,000 trees, planted around the Tidal Basin.

questions.q: How tall is the Washington Monument, the tallest structure in the city?
questions.explain: A law from 1910 keeps other buildings lower, so the obelisk still rules the skyline.

questions.q: Which ancient Inca site did you visit, high in the Andes at about 7,970 feet?
questions.explain: Cusco, where that adventure began, is even higher: about 11,150 feet above sea level.

questions.q: Which rose-red city was the capital of the Nabataeans more than two thousand years ago?
questions.explain: Its famous Treasury is carved straight into the cliff.

questions.q: In which year did Tokyo give the first cherry trees to Washington?
questions.explain: About 3,000 trees arrived that year. Tokyo sent a second gift in 1965.

questions.q: You said "Iorana" on which island?
questions.explain: Iorana means both hello and goodbye in Rapa Nui.

questions.q: In Morocco, which drink is poured from a height into small glasses as a welcome?
questions.explain: Pouring from high up cools the tea a little and makes a light foam on top.

questions.q: Which animals fill the plains of the Serengeti in the Great Migration?
questions.explain: More than a million wildebeest, with zebras and gazelles, follow the rains in a great circle through Tanzania and Kenya.

questions.q: How long is the Great Barrier Reef along the coast of Queensland?
questions.explain: It is the largest coral reef system in the world, made of thousands of separate reefs and islands.

questions.q: Which creamy, mild curry steamed in a banana leaf is Cambodia's best-known dish?
questions.explain: Amok is flavored with lemongrass, galangal and coconut milk.

questions.q: Which dish of chilies cooked in cheese is the national dish of Bhutan?
questions.explain: It is eaten with red rice, and it is spicy: in Bhutan, chilies are a vegetable, not a spice.

etiquette: Tell the people at home one thing you learned in each place: it keeps the memory alive.
Write a kind note to a guide or driver who made your day: it helps their work more than you think.

destinations.name: Cusco
facts: Cusco means "navel" in Quechua: the Inca saw their capital as the centre of the world.
The Inca built about 40,000 km of roads across the Andes. Many are still walked today.
At 3,400 m the air holds about a third less oxygen. Coca tea is the local remedy.

greeting.meaning: "Are you well?" A warm everyday greeting in the language of the Inca.

facts: Elevation 11,150 ft

steps.title: The Inca Trail
steps.blurb: Guide your llama up to the Sun Gate.
steps.intro: Your llama carries the picnic up to Inti Punku, the Sun Gate above Machu Picchu. Tap the screen or press Space to jump over rocks, and grab the woven textiles. Three stumbles and the llama lies down.
steps.fact: The classic Inca Trail is about 26 miles long. Hikers reach Machu Picchu through Inti Punku, the Sun Gate, on the last morning.

steps.title: Master mason
steps.blurb: Find the stones that fit the wall, Inca style.
steps.intro: Inca masons fitted stones so tightly that they needed no mortar. For each gap in the wall, pick the one stone that fits exactly. Five gaps; four right first time earns a star.
steps.fact: In Cusco, on Hatun Rumiyoc street, the famous Twelve-Angled Stone fits perfectly against all of its neighbors. Masons shaped it with harder hammerstones, testing the fit again and again.

questions.q: Machu Picchu was built as a royal estate for which Inca ruler?
questions.explain: Most archaeologists date it to the mid-1400s, built for the emperor Pachacuti. Atahualpa and Huáscar were brothers who fought a civil war about a century later.

questions.q: What holds the finest Inca stone walls together?
questions.right: Nothing: the stones are cut to fit
questions.explain: Inca masons shaped each block to fit its neighbors so tightly that a knife blade cannot slip between them. No mortar at all.

questions.q: In 1911, who brought Machu Picchu to international attention?
questions.explain: Local farmers guided the Yale lecturer Hiram Bingham to the site, which they had always known. His later excavations were supported by the NGE Society.

questions.q: How did the world first see Machu Picchu in detail?
questions.right: A whole issue of NGE magazine, in April 1913
questions.explain: After Hiram Bingham’s 1912 excavation, sponsored by Yale and the NGE Society, the magazine gave its entire April 1913 issue to Machu Picchu, with his photographs.

questions.q: What did the Inca call their empire?
questions.explain: Tawantinsuyu means roughly "the four parts together" in Quechua: four regions meeting in Cusco. Qhapaq Ñan is the name of their great road network.

questions.q: What is Inti Raymi, celebrated in Cusco every 24 June?
questions.explain: It honors Inti, the sun god, around the southern winter solstice. Banned under Spanish rule, it was revived as a great re-enactment in 1944.

questions.q: What were quipus?
questions.right: Knotted cords used to keep records
questions.explain: The type and position of each knot recorded numbers, like tribute and census counts. Researchers are still studying whether they also recorded words.

questions.q: Which Andean animal is raised mainly for its soft fleece?
questions.explain: Llamas are larger and were bred mostly to carry loads. Alpacas are smaller and bred for fleece. The wild vicuña has the finest fibre of all.

questions.q: Which river winds through the valley below Machu Picchu?
questions.explain: The Urubamba flows through the Sacred Valley and loops around the mountain. Far downstream, its waters do join the Amazon.

questions.q: What is chuño?
questions.explain: Farmers leave potatoes out through freezing nights and sunny days, then press out the water. Chuño keeps for years. Peru grows thousands of potato varieties.

questions.q: Many Cusco hotels offer a traditional drink for the altitude. Which one?
questions.explain: Mate de coca is a mild herbal tea, legal in Peru and part of Andean life for centuries. Chicha morada is a sweet purple corn drink, delicious but not for altitude.

etiquette: Ask before you photograph people in traditional dress. Some families in Cusco pose for visitors and expect a small tip, others prefer not to be photographed.
Take your first day at altitude slowly: walk gently, drink plenty of water, and try a cup of mate de coca.

destinations.name: Easter Island
facts: There are almost 900 moai on Rapa Nui. Most were carved in a single volcanic quarry.
The nearest inhabited island, Pitcairn, is about 2,000 km away. This is one of the most remote places on Earth.
Rapa Nui stories say the moai "walked" to their platforms. Engineers have shown they really can be rocked upright, step by step.

greeting.meaning: "Hello!" It also means goodbye, so you can use it all day.

facts: 2,200 miles from mainland Chile

steps.title: The first egg
steps.blurb: Catch the sooty tern eggs on Motu Nui.
steps.intro: In the Birdman competition, champions swam to the islet of Motu Nui and waited for the first sooty tern egg of the season. Drag left and right (or use the arrow keys) to catch the eggs the terns drop, and dodge the loose stones. Catch 12. Three slips and another chief wins.
steps.fact: From Orongo, competitors climbed down the cliffs and swam to Motu Nui to wait for the first sooty tern egg of the season. The winner’s chief became the Tangata manu, the Birdman, for a year.

steps.title: Walk the moai
steps.blurb: Rock the statue forward with the ropes.
steps.intro: Legend says the moai walked to their platforms. Teams with ropes rocked them from side to side, step by step. Tap the left or right side as each beat reaches the line (or use the arrow keys).
steps.fact: Rapa Nui oral tradition says the moai walked. In 2012, archaeologists Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo, with NGE support, showed that a team with three ropes could rock a replica moai forward, upright, step by step.

questions.q: What are the stone platforms that moai stand on called?
questions.explain: An ahu is a ceremonial stone platform. Most moai stood on ahu facing inland, watching over their village. Pukao are the red stone topknots some moai wear.

questions.q: From which volcano’s quarry were most moai carved?
questions.explain: Nearly all moai were carved from the volcanic tuff of Rano Raraku. Hundreds still lie in and around the quarry, some unfinished.

questions.q: Who gave Easter Island its European name?
questions.explain: The Dutch explorer landed on Easter Sunday 1722. The islanders call their home Rapa Nui, and it has been part of Chile since 1888.

questions.q: What is rongorongo?
questions.right: A script on wooden tablets, still undeciphered
questions.explain: About two dozen rongorongo objects survive in museums around the world. No one has yet been able to read them.

questions.q: What did the Birdman competitors race to bring back?
questions.right: The first sooty tern egg of the season
questions.explain: They swam to the islet of Motu Nui and waited for the first egg. The winner’s chief became the Tangata manu, the Birdman, for a year.

questions.q: What is Tapati Rapa Nui, held each February?
questions.right: A festival of Rapa Nui culture
questions.explain: Families compete in music, dance and traditional sports, including haka pei: sliding down a steep hillside on banana-trunk sleds.

questions.q: Roughly how far is Easter Island from mainland Chile?
questions.explain: It is one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth. The nearest inhabited island, Pitcairn, is about 1,300 miles away.

questions.q: At which beach is the founding chief Hotu Matu’a said to have landed?
questions.explain: Oral tradition says Hotu Matu’a landed at Anakena. Today its white sand and palms face the restored moai of Ahu Nau Nau.

questions.q: What is an umu?
questions.explain: Food is wrapped in banana leaves and cooked on hot stones buried in the ground. An umu is often the heart of a celebration.

questions.q: Which tuber, native to South America, was a staple on Rapa Nui long before Europeans arrived?
questions.explain: Sweet potato, kumara in Polynesian languages, comes from South America. Its spread across Polynesia suggests contact with South America centuries before Europeans.

etiquette: Never touch or climb on the moai or their stone platforms. They are sacred, and it is forbidden by law.
Stay on the marked paths: many archaeological sites lie hidden in the grass.

destinations.name: Apia
facts: In 2011 Samoa skipped a whole day, 30 December, when it moved to the other side of the International Date Line.
Robert Louis Stevenson lived in Samoa for his last four years and is buried on Mount Vaea, above Apia.
A traditional Samoan fale has no walls: the roof shades, and the breeze does the rest.

greeting.meaning: "Hello!" Often answered with a smile and "Tālofa lava".

facts: Highest point 6,096 ft

steps.title: Fa’ataupati
steps.blurb: Keep the beat of the slap dance.
steps.intro: The fa’ataupati is Samoa’s famous slap dance. Tap left and right as each beat reaches the line, or use the arrow keys. Stay sharp: the drum speeds up!
steps.fact: The fa’ataupati is danced by men slapping their bodies in rhythm. It is often said to imitate swatting mosquitoes.

steps.title: Siapo patterns
steps.blurb: Complete the tapa cloth designs.
steps.intro: Siapo is bark cloth decorated with bold, balanced patterns. Finish each design by mirroring the left half on the right: tap a square to change its color. Three designs.
steps.fact: Siapo is made from the inner bark of the paper mulberry tree, beaten thin and painted with natural dyes. It is still given as a gift at important ceremonies.

questions.q: What is a fale?
questions.explain: Its open sides let the sea breeze through. Woven blinds can be lowered when it rains.

questions.q: Which famous writer spent his last years at Vailima, near Apia?
questions.explain: The author of Treasure Island died there in 1894. Samoans called him Tusitala, "teller of tales", and he is buried on Mount Vaea above the house.

questions.q: In 1962, Samoa became the first Pacific island nation to…
questions.explain: Samoa regained independence from New Zealand on 1 January 1962, the first Pacific island nation to do so in the 20th century.

questions.q: In 2011, Samoa skipped a whole day. Why?
questions.right: It moved to the other side of the date line
questions.explain: Friday 30 December 2011 never happened in Samoa. The country jumped west of the International Date Line to match its trading partners, Australia and New Zealand.

questions.q: What does fa’a Samoa mean?
questions.explain: It centers on the aiga, the extended family, led by matai, chiefs chosen by the family, with respect and service to the community.

questions.q: What is the traditional men’s tattoo from waist to knees called?
questions.explain: The pe’a is applied with hand tools over several days, a mark of courage and service. The women’s tattoo is the malu.

questions.q: What are the Alofaaga blowholes on Savai’i famous for?
questions.right: Seawater shooting high through the lava rock
questions.explain: Waves force water up through holes in the old lava shelf, sending spray dozens of feet into the air. Locals throw in coconuts to watch them fly.

questions.q: What is To Sua Ocean Trench?
questions.right: A deep swimming hole reached by a long ladder
questions.explain: Its name means "giant swimming hole". A lava tunnel links it to the ocean, so the water rises and falls with the tides.

questions.q: What is palusami?
questions.right: Taro leaves with coconut cream, baked in the umu
questions.explain: Young taro leaves are wrapped around rich coconut cream and cooked in the umu, the earth oven, often for the big Sunday meal, to’ona’i.

questions.q: What is oka?
questions.right: Raw fish in citrus and coconut cream
questions.explain: Fresh fish is "cooked" in lime or lemon juice, then mixed with coconut cream, onion and a little chilli.

etiquette: Sunday is for church and family. Keep noise down, dress modestly, and avoid swimming near villages that day.
In a fale, sit cross-legged and don’t point your feet at anyone. Avoid eating while walking through a village.

destinations.name: Port Douglas
facts: The Great Barrier Reef is made of about 2,900 separate reefs and is large enough to be seen from space.
The Daintree Rainforest is about 180 million years old, older than the Amazon.
The reef is alive: its corals are tiny animals that live together in colonies.
About 1,400 miles long

steps.title: Home to the anemone
steps.blurb: Swim the clownfish through the coral.
steps.intro: Your clownfish has wandered off. Tap anywhere (or press Space) to swim up, and let go to sink. Slip through the gaps between the coral and the jellyfish, all the way home to the anemone. 15 gaps.
steps.fact: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones. A layer of mucus protects them from the stings, and the anemone protects them from predators. Never touch the coral: even a light touch harms the living polyps.

steps.title: Masters of disguise
steps.blurb: Find five camouflaged creatures.
steps.intro: Five creatures are hiding on this patch of reef, perfectly camouflaged. Tap each one when you spot it. Tip: look for the eyes.
steps.fact: Octopuses and cuttlefish change color and skin texture in a fraction of a second. The reef stonefish is the most venomous fish known, which is why reef shoes matter.

questions.q: In which year did the Great Barrier Reef become a UNESCO World Heritage site?
questions.explain: It was one of the first natural sites listed in Australia. The protected area covers about 134,000 square miles.

questions.q: What actually builds the reef?
questions.explain: Each polyp builds a hard limestone skeleton. Over thousands of years, billions of them build reefs. Most get their color from algae living inside them.

questions.q: Which explorer’s ship struck the reef in 1770?
questions.explain: The Endeavour ran aground near today’s Cape Tribulation. Cook beached it for repairs at the river now called the Endeavour River, at Cooktown.

questions.q: Who have cared for the reef’s sea country for tens of thousands of years?
questions.right: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.explain: More than 70 Traditional Owner groups have connections to the Great Barrier Reef region.

questions.q: In Australian slang, what is the "arvo"?
questions.explain: Australians love shortening words: arvo for afternoon, brekkie for breakfast, sunnies for sunglasses.

questions.q: Around Port Douglas, the rainforest country belongs to which Aboriginal people?
questions.explain: Eastern Kuku Yalanji country runs from the rainforest to the sea. At Mossman Gorge, Kuku Yalanji guides lead walks and share their culture.

questions.q: Mass coral spawning happens a few nights after…
questions.right: A full moon in late spring
questions.explain: On cue, corals release billions of eggs and sperm at once, like an underwater snowstorm. It usually happens in November or December.

questions.q: Which turtle nests on Raine Island in the largest numbers on Earth?
questions.explain: Raine Island, in the far northern reef, is the largest known green turtle nesting site in the world.

questions.q: What is Vegemite?
questions.explain: Australians spread it very thinly on buttered toast. A thick layer is the classic beginner’s mistake.

questions.q: What is a barramundi?
questions.explain: Barramundi is a prized fish of northern Australia’s rivers and coasts, often grilled. Its name comes from an Aboriginal language.

etiquette: Wear a stinger suit when swimming from about November to May: it protects you from jellyfish and the sun.
Don’t touch, stand on or kick the coral, and keep a respectful distance from turtles.

destinations.name: Siem Reap
facts: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world. It was built in about 30 years, in the 12th century.
Ta Prohm was left almost as the jungle claimed it. It appears in the film Tomb Raider.
Every year the Tonlé Sap river changes direction: it flows towards the lake in the dry season and away from it in the rainy season.

greeting.meaning: A respectful hello, said with palms together in a sampeah.

facts: Temple park over 150 sq miles

steps.title: The dancing apsaras
steps.blurb: Find the celestial dancers in the carved wall.
steps.intro: Find the five apsaras, the celestial dancers, hidden among the standing devatas carved in the wall. Tip: apsaras dance, with bent knees and a pointed crown.
steps.fact: Angkor Wat’s walls show nearly 1,800 carved women. Most are devatas, standing goddesses; the dancing ones are apsaras. No two wear quite the same headdress.

steps.title: Cook fish amok
steps.blurb: Follow the chef’s order of ingredients.
steps.intro: A Cambodian chef shows you how to make kroeung, the paste at the heart of fish amok. Watch the ingredients she adds, then tap them in the same order. Each round adds one more.
steps.fact: Fish amok is steamed in banana-leaf cups with kroeung, a paste of lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and kaffir lime leaf, plus rich coconut milk.

questions.q: Angkor Wat was first built as a temple to which Hindu god?
questions.explain: King Suryavarman II built it in the early 12th century for Vishnu. It later became a Buddhist temple, which it still is.

questions.q: Which temple is famous for giant trees growing through its ruins?
questions.explain: Strangler figs and silk-cotton trees wrap their roots around Ta Prohm’s walls. It was deliberately left much as explorers found it.

questions.q: The Bayon temple is famous for its…
questions.explain: The Bayon was built around 1200 under King Jayavarman VII. Its towers carry about 200 smiling faces, which many think portray the king himself.

questions.q: Angkor was the capital of which empire?
questions.explain: From the 9th to the 15th century, the Khmer Empire ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from Angkor, one of the largest cities of its time.

questions.q: How do Cambodians traditionally greet each other?
questions.right: Palms together with a slight bow, the sampeah
questions.explain: The higher the hands, the more respect shown: highest for monks and elders.

questions.q: When is Khmer New Year, Choul Chnam Thmey, celebrated?
questions.explain: It marks the end of the harvest before the rains. Families visit pagodas, and friends splash each other with water.

questions.q: Which lake near Siem Reap reverses its flow every year?
questions.explain: In the rainy season the Mekong pushes water back up the Tonlé Sap river, and the lake swells to several times its dry-season size.

questions.q: What happens at Angkor Wat at sunrise around the spring equinox?
questions.right: The sun rises right above the central tower
questions.explain: Angkor Wat faces west. At the equinoxes, seen from the western entrance, the sun appears directly over its central tower.

questions.q: What is kroeung?
questions.right: A Khmer paste of lemongrass, galangal and turmeric
questions.explain: Kroeung is pounded by hand in a mortar and flavours many Khmer dishes, including fish amok.

questions.q: Cambodia’s famous pepper comes from which province?
questions.explain: Kampot pepper has a protected geographical indication, like Champagne in France.

etiquette: Cover shoulders and knees to enter the temples. Guards check before you climb Angkor Wat’s upper level.
Never touch anyone’s head, and don’t point your feet at people or at Buddha images.

destinations.name: Kathmandu
facts: Seven groups of monuments in the Kathmandu Valley are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, in a space you can cross in an hour.
Nepal has the only national flag in the world that is not a rectangle.
The Kumari, a young girl chosen as a living goddess, lives in a palace on Durbar Square.

greeting.meaning: "I bow to you." Said with the palms pressed together, to say hello and goodbye.

facts: Elevation 4,600 ft

steps.title: Roof of the world
steps.blurb: Spot the Himalayan animals your guide names.
steps.intro: The valley is ringed by mountains, and the forests above it hide some shy neighbors. Your guide names an animal: tap it as soon as you see it among the others. Take your time, there is no clock to beat.
steps.fact: Nepal shares or holds eight of the fourteen mountains in the world that rise above 26,247 feet, among them Mount Everest at 29,032 feet.

steps.title: Mandala maker
steps.blurb: Complete the other half of the sacred pattern.
steps.intro: Artists in the Kathmandu Valley have painted mandalas for centuries. A mandala is balanced: what happens on one side happens on the other. Finish the right half so it mirrors the left.
steps.fact: A mandala is a map for meditation. Some are painted on cloth, others made of colored sand that is swept away when finished, a lesson in impermanence.

questions.q: The great stupa of Boudhanath is painted with a pair of watchful eyes. Whose eyes are they?
questions.explain: Wise eyes look out in the four directions from the tower above the dome. The mark between them is the Nepali number one, a symbol of unity.

questions.q: Which river runs beside the Hindu temple complex of Pashupatinath?
questions.explain: The Bagmati flows through the Kathmandu Valley. Pashupatinath, dedicated to Shiva, stands on its banks and is among the holiest Hindu sites in Nepal.

questions.q: What does "Durbar" mean in Durbar Square?
questions.explain: Kathmandu's Durbar Square grew around the palaces of the Malla and Shah kings. There are Durbar Squares in Patan and Bhaktapur too.

questions.q: What struck Nepal on April 25, 2015, damaging many temples in the Kathmandu Valley?
questions.explain: Many monuments have been rebuilt since, with traditional methods and materials, by local craftspeople.

questions.q: Who is the Kumari of Kathmandu?
questions.right: A young girl honored as a living goddess
questions.explain: The Royal Kumari lives in a house beside Durbar Square and is chosen as a small child. She is cared for with great respect and returns to ordinary life when she grows up.

questions.q: What do the colorful flags strung across Himalayan passes and temples carry?
questions.right: Prayers and good wishes, spread by the wind
questions.explain: Prayer flags come in five colors: blue, white, red, green and yellow. The wind carries their blessings to everyone.

questions.q: What is the highest mountain on Earth?
questions.explain: Everest rises about 29,032 feet above sea level. In Nepali it is Sagarmatha, and in Tibetan Chomolungma.

questions.q: Which animal with a reddish-brown coat and a ringed tail lives in the bamboo forests of the Himalaya?
questions.explain: Red pandas live in cool forests of eastern Nepal and neighboring countries. They are not close relatives of the giant panda.

questions.q: Which meal do most people in Nepal eat once or twice a day?
questions.right: Dal bhat: lentil soup with rice and side dishes
questions.explain: Dal bhat is the everyday meal. A common saying goes: "Dal bhat power, 24 hour!"

questions.q: What are momos?
questions.explain: Momos are popular across Kathmandu, usually filled with vegetables or meat and served with a spicy tomato sauce.

etiquette: Greet people with your palms together and a small bow: "Namaste."
Walk clockwise around stupas and prayer wheels, and take your shoes off before entering temples. Do not touch anyone on the head.
Some inner sanctuaries of Hindu temples are for worshippers only. Your guide will tell you where to stop. Ask before photographing people.

destinations.name: Paro
facts: Bhutan measures its progress in Gross National Happiness, not only in money.
Paro airport is among the most demanding in the world: only a small group of pilots are trained to land here.
Bhutan absorbs more carbon than it produces. Forest covers more than two thirds of the country.

greeting.meaning: "Hello!" The "la" at the end adds respect.

facts: Tiger’s Nest 10,240 ft

steps.title: Archery
steps.blurb: Bhutan’s national sport: six arrows at the target.
steps.intro: Archery is Bhutan’s national sport. Your sight sways with your breathing: tap (or press Space) to shoot when it’s over the bullseye. Watch the prayer flag, because the wind pushes your arrow. Six arrows.
steps.fact: Archery became Bhutan’s national sport in 1971. In traditional matches, the targets stand about 475 ft apart, and when an archer hits, teammates dance and sing in front of the target.

steps.title: Raise the prayer flags
steps.blurb: Hang the colors in the order the monk shows.
steps.intro: Prayer flags come in five colors, one for each element. Watch the order the monk hangs them, then repeat it. Each round adds one more flag.
steps.fact: Lungta, "wind horse" flags, come in five colors: blue for space, white for air, red for fire, green for water, yellow for earth. The wind is said to carry their prayers.

questions.q: What is a dzong?
questions.right: A fortress-monastery that also houses government offices
questions.explain: Dzongs like Paro’s Rinpung Dzong combine monks’ quarters with district administration, under one roof.

questions.q: Tiger’s Nest is linked to which teacher who brought Buddhism to Bhutan?
questions.explain: Also called Padmasambhava, he is said to have flown to the cliff on a tigress and meditated in a cave there.

questions.q: What does Bhutan famously measure, not just GDP?
questions.explain: The idea is credited to the fourth king in the 1970s. Bhutan’s policies weigh wellbeing, culture and nature, not only growth.

questions.q: What do the Bhutanese call their country?
questions.right: Druk Yul, "Land of the Thunder Dragon"
questions.explain: The thunder dragon, Druk, appears on the national flag.

questions.q: What is the national dress for men called?
questions.explain: The gho is a knee-length robe tied with a belt; women wear the kira. Both are worn at work, at school and at festivals.

questions.q: What happens at a tshechu festival?
questions.right: Masked dances in the dzong courtyard
questions.explain: Tshechus honor Guru Rinpoche. On the last morning in Paro, a giant thangka, a sacred painting, is unrolled before sunrise.

questions.q: What covers most of Bhutan?
questions.explain: The constitution requires at least 60% forest cover to be kept for all time. Today about 70% of the country is forest.

questions.q: What is the national animal of Bhutan?
questions.explain: The takin looks like a cross between a goat and a cow. Legend credits its odd shape to Drukpa Kunley, the "Divine Madman".

questions.q: What is ema datshi, the national dish?
questions.explain: In Bhutan, chillies are treated as a vegetable, not a spice. Ema means chilli, datshi means cheese.

questions.q: Which rice is a Bhutanese speciality?
questions.explain: Bhutanese red rice grows at high altitude. It is nutty and slightly sticky, and served with almost every meal.

etiquette: Walk clockwise around temples, chortens and prayer wheels, and turn the wheels clockwise.
Dress modestly in dzongs and temples: long sleeves, no hats, and shoes off where asked.

destinations.name: Agra
facts: The Taj Mahal took about 20 years and thousands of workers to build, for an emperor's wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
The white marble seems to change colour during the day: pink at dawn, white at noon, golden at sunset.
The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan could see the Taj Mahal from his room in Agra Fort in his last years.

greeting.meaning: "I bow to you." Said with palms pressed together.

facts: On the Yamuna river

steps.title: Perfect symmetry
steps.blurb: Mirror the Taj Mahal’s inlay design.
steps.intro: Everything at the Taj Mahal mirrors itself around a central axis. Complete each inlay design so the right half mirrors the left: tap a square to change its stone. Three designs, against the clock.
steps.fact: The Taj Mahal is almost perfectly symmetrical. The one exception is Shah Jahan’s own cenotaph, placed beside Mumtaz Mahal’s when he was buried there in 1666.

steps.title: Pietra dura
steps.blurb: Set the gemstones into the marble.
steps.intro: Mughal craftsmen cut semi-precious stones to fit hollows carved in the marble, so precisely that the joins are almost invisible. Pick the stone that fits each hollow. Four right first time earns a star.
steps.fact: Carnelian, lapis lazuli, jade and other stones were inlaid into the Taj Mahal’s marble. Families in Agra still practice this craft today.

questions.q: Who built the Taj Mahal, and for whom?
questions.right: Shah Jahan, for his wife Mumtaz Mahal
questions.explain: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631. Shah Jahan built her mausoleum over about two decades.

questions.q: Why does the Taj Mahal seem to change color during the day?
questions.right: Its white marble reflects the changing light
questions.explain: It glows pinkish at dawn, white at noon and golden at sunset. The marble came from Makrana, in Rajasthan.

questions.q: Agra Fort is built mostly of what?
questions.explain: Emperor Akbar rebuilt it in red sandstone from 1565. Shah Jahan later spent his last years there, with a view of the Taj.

questions.q: Who founded the Mughal dynasty in India in 1526?
questions.explain: Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, won the Battle of Panipat in 1526. Agra became one of the Mughal capitals.

questions.q: What does namaste, with palms together, express?
questions.right: A respectful greeting: "I bow to you"
questions.explain: From Sanskrit, it works as hello and goodbye, and avoids touching.

questions.q: What does Holi, the festival of colors, celebrate?
questions.right: The arrival of spring and good over evil
questions.explain: People throw colored powder and water at each other. Nearby Mathura and Vrindavan are famous for their Holi celebrations.

questions.q: Which river flows right behind the Taj Mahal?
questions.explain: The Yamuna joins the Ganges further east, at Prayagraj. From the far bank, the Mehtab Bagh garden offers a quiet view of the Taj.

questions.q: What is India’s national bird, common in the countryside around Agra?
questions.explain: Indian peafowl roam fields and gardens across Uttar Pradesh. The male’s shimmering train is full of "eyes".

questions.q: Agra is famous for petha. What is it?
questions.right: A translucent sweet made from ash gourd
questions.explain: Petha is boiled in sugar syrup until it turns crystal clear, sometimes flavoured with rose or saffron.

questions.q: What is a thali?
questions.right: A platter of many small dishes
questions.explain: A thali brings dal, vegetables, rice, bread, pickles and a sweet, so you taste a little of everything in one meal.

etiquette: Shoes come off (or covers go on) before the mausoleum. The Taj Mahal is closed to visitors on Fridays.
Greet with namaste rather than a handshake, especially with women, and eat with your right hand.

destinations.name: Serengeti
facts: Serengeti means "endless plains" in the language of the Maasai.
About 1.5 million wildebeest follow the rains round the Serengeti every year.
A lion can sleep up to 20 hours a day. Most hunting is done at dusk and dawn.

greeting.meaning: "Hello!" The friendly greeting you’ll hear on every safari.

facts: Plains 3,000 to 6,000 ft

steps.title: Photo safari
steps.blurb: Snap the animals the guide calls out.
steps.intro: Your guide calls out an animal: tap it to take the photo. Wrong animal and the guide sighs. Snap 8 before the light goes.
steps.fact: Each year about 1.5 million wildebeest, with hundreds of thousands of zebras and gazelles, circle between the Serengeti and Kenya’s Maasai Mara, following the rains.

steps.title: The adumu
steps.blurb: Jump on the beat of the song.
steps.intro: In the adumu, Maasai warriors take turns jumping as high as they can while the others sing. Tap (or press Space) exactly on each beat to jump higher.
steps.fact: The adumu is part of Eunoto, the ceremony when young Maasai warriors become senior warriors. The circle sings while each jumper tries to go highest.

questions.q: What does "Serengeti" mean in the Maa language?
questions.explain: It comes from the Maasai word siringet, the place where the land runs on forever.

questions.q: What is the Ngorongoro Crater?
questions.right: A huge collapsed volcano, or caldera
questions.explain: It is about 12 miles across, and its floor is home to around 25,000 large animals, including rare black rhinos.

questions.q: Olduvai Gorge, near the Serengeti, is famous for…
questions.right: Early human fossils and stone tools
questions.explain: Louis and Mary Leakey’s discoveries there, supported by the NGE Society, reshaped our picture of human origins.

questions.q: Which researcher began studying wild chimpanzees in Tanzania in 1960, with support from the NGE Society soon after?
questions.explain: Jane Goodall’s work at Gombe, on Lake Tanganyika, showed that chimpanzees make and use tools. NGE began supporting her research in 1961.

questions.q: Who was Tanzania’s first president, who championed Swahili as a national language?
questions.explain: Nyerere, known as Mwalimu, "the teacher", led the country from independence. Swahili helped unite more than 120 ethnic groups.

questions.q: What is the cloth Maasai often wear called?
questions.explain: Red shukas stand out against the savannah. Bright beadwork shows age, status and family.

questions.q: "Hakuna matata" really is Swahili. What does it mean?
questions.explain: Swahili is spoken by tens of millions of people across East Africa. Pole pole, "slowly slowly", is another phrase you’ll hear on safari.

questions.q: What does the great migration follow?
questions.explain: The herds circle clockwise between Tanzania and Kenya, chasing new grass. Lions, hyenas and crocodiles follow them.

questions.q: Which mountain, Africa’s highest at 19,341 ft, stands in northern Tanzania?
questions.explain: Kilimanjaro is a dormant volcano, and its summit glaciers are shrinking fast.

questions.q: What is ugali?
questions.right: A stiff maize porridge eaten with the hands
questions.explain: Pull off a piece, roll it into a ball, and press a dent with your thumb to scoop up stews and greens.

questions.q: What does nyama choma mean?
questions.explain: Usually goat or beef, slow-grilled over charcoal and shared with friends, often with kachumbari, a fresh tomato and onion salad.

etiquette: Always ask before photographing Maasai people or their villages; many will ask a fee, which is fair.
On game drives, stay inside the vehicle and keep your voice low: the animals are wild, even when they seem calm.

destinations.name: Petra
facts: Petra was unknown to the western world until 1812, when a Swiss explorer disguised himself to reach it.
The Treasury is carved straight into the cliff and is about 40 metres high.
The Nabataeans lived in the desert by catching every drop of rain in channels and cisterns.

greeting.meaning: "Hello!" Often answered with "marhabtein", two hellos back.

facts: Monastery: about 800 steps up

steps.title: Carve the Treasury
steps.blurb: Cut Al-Khazneh out of the cliff, top down.
steps.intro: Drag your finger across the cliff to cut away the rock and reveal the Treasury. Work like the Nabataean masons: from the top down. Each level opens once the one above is clear. 90 seconds.
steps.fact: Nabataean masons carved Petra’s facades from the top down, standing on the uncut rock below them, so they needed little or no scaffolding. The Treasury is about 130 ft tall.

steps.title: Water for the city
steps.blurb: Turn the channel stones to fill the cistern.
steps.intro: Petra gets very little rain, so every drop counted. Tap the channel stones to turn them until the water flows from the dam all the way to the cistern. Three channels, each a little longer.
steps.fact: The Nabataeans built dams, channels and cisterns to catch the rare rain and protect the city from flash floods. Clay pipes carried water along the walls of the Siq.

questions.q: Petra’s most famous facade, Al-Khazneh, is usually called…
questions.explain: Legend said treasure was hidden in the urn at the top, which is why it is scarred by bullets. It was most likely a royal tomb.

questions.q: How were Petra’s great facades made?
questions.right: Carved directly into the rock cliffs
questions.explain: Nabataean masons worked from the top of the cliff downwards, carving away the rock around each facade.

questions.q: Who built Petra?
questions.explain: These Arab traders grew rich on incense and spice caravans. Rome annexed their kingdom in 106 AD.

questions.q: Which Swiss explorer revealed Petra to the Western world in 1812?
questions.explain: Traveling as a scholar called Sheikh Ibrahim, he persuaded a guide to take him there.

questions.q: What does "ahlan wa sahlan" mean?
questions.explain: Jordanian hospitality is legendary: expect to hear it often, and to be offered tea or coffee.

questions.q: Which Bedouin tribe lived in Petra’s caves until the 1980s?
questions.explain: When Petra became a protected site, most Bdul families moved to the nearby village of Umm Sayhoun. Many still work in Petra today.

questions.q: Why is Petra called the Rose City?
questions.explain: Iron and other minerals streak the rock in pink, red, orange and violet.

questions.q: How did the Nabataeans get water in the desert?
questions.right: Dams, channels and cisterns for the rare rain
questions.explain: Channels carved along the Siq carried water into the city, and dams protected it from flash floods.

questions.q: Mansaf, Jordan’s national dish, is lamb cooked in…
questions.explain: It is served on rice and flatbread on a big shared platter, traditionally eaten with the right hand.

questions.q: Bedouin coffee is spiced with…
questions.explain: It is light, fragrant and served in small handleless cups, a few sips at a time.

etiquette: Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees, especially outside the tourist areas.
Accept coffee or tea when offered. When you’ve had enough coffee, gently shake the small cup before handing it back.

destinations.name: Marrakech
facts: Marrakech is called the Red City because of the colour of its walls, built from local clay.
The Jemaa el-Fna square is recognised by UNESCO for its living traditions: storytellers, musicians and food stalls.
Moroccan mint tea is poured from a height to make it foam. A good host pours it high.

greeting.meaning: "Hello!" The greeting of the Amazigh people of the Atlas.

facts: Elevation 1,530 ft

steps.title: Lost in the souks
steps.blurb: Find the family’s door before the tea gets cold.
steps.intro: A Berber family has invited the group for mint tea, somewhere deep in the medina. Follow the glow of their lantern and pick up fresh mint on the way. Swipe, use the arrows below, or your keyboard.
steps.fact: The medina of Marrakech has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1985. Its souks are grouped by craft: dyers, metalworkers, leather, spices.

steps.title: The tea ceremony
steps.blurb: Pour three glasses from high, just to the line.
steps.intro: Hold to pour and release when the tea reaches the gold line. The longer you pour, the higher the pot rises and the better the foam. Don’t overflow! Three glasses: gentle as life, strong as love, bitter as death.
steps.fact: Moroccan mint tea is green tea brewed with fresh spearmint and plenty of sugar. Green tea became popular in Morocco through British trade in the 1800s.

questions.q: Which dynasty built the Koutoubia Mosque, whose minaret rises over Marrakech?
questions.explain: The Almohads completed it in the 12th century. Its minaret inspired later towers, including the Giralda in Seville. The Ottomans never ruled Morocco.

questions.q: Jemaa el-Fnaa, the great square, is famous for what?
questions.explain: In 2001, UNESCO named the square a masterpiece of oral and intangible heritage for its storytellers and performers, one of the first places honored this way.

questions.q: Around what year was Marrakech founded?
questions.explain: The Almoravids founded it around 1070. The city gave its name to the whole country: "Morocco" comes from "Marrakech".

questions.q: Why is Marrakech nicknamed the Red City?
questions.right: Its walls are built of red-ochre earth
wrong: Its old royal flag was red
questions.explain: The ramparts were built of rammed earth rich in local red clay. Many buildings are still painted in the same warm ochre.

questions.q: Why is mint tea poured from high above the glass?
questions.right: To make a little foam and mix it
questions.explain: Pouring from height aerates the tea and builds a small foam on top, the sign of a well-made glass.

questions.q: A popular saying describes three glasses of tea. The first is gentle as life, the second strong as love, the third is…
questions.explain: Each glass steeps a little longer, so the taste changes. Guests are expected to take all three.

questions.q: Which mountains rise on the horizon south of Marrakech?
questions.explain: The High Atlas is snow-capped in winter and home to many Amazigh villages. Toubkal, North Africa’s highest peak at 13,671 ft, is about 40 miles away.

questions.q: The Majorelle Garden is famous for an intense shade of which color?
questions.explain: The painter Jacques Majorelle created the garden from 1923 and painted his studio a vivid cobalt blue. Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé later restored it.

questions.q: What is a tagine?
questions.right: A slow-cooked stew and its cone-lidded clay pot
questions.explain: The cone shape sends steam back down onto the food, so it stays moist with very little water.

questions.q: Sharing food from a communal plate, which hand do you eat with?
questions.explain: The right hand is used for eating and greeting. Bread often serves as your spoon.

etiquette: When tea is offered, accept it and take the glass with your right hand. Refusing can feel like refusing the welcome.
In the souks, bargaining is expected and friendly. Smile, take your time, and only make an offer if you really want to buy.

options.name: Departure briefing and welcome reception
options.difficulty_note: Seated and standing at a reception. No walking.
options.description: Tonight the expedition begins. Over a drink, you meet the people who will share the next 25 days, hear how the journey unfolds, and look at the map that is about to turn into memories. Ask everything you want. By the end of the evening, the round-the-world flight will feel real.
options.bring: Smart casual.
options.accessibility: On one level, seated or standing, with a lift from the lobby to the ballroom floor. Step-free.

options.name: Altitude orientation walk
options.difficulty_note: A slow 1 km stroll on flat ground at 3,400 m above sea level. The air is thin: go slowly and drink water.
options.description: Today we take our first slow steps at 3,400 metres. We wander the old streets of Cusco at the pace of the thin air, stop in a sunlit courtyard for a cup of coca tea, and let our bodies learn the Andes. It is the gentlest way to start one of the great adventures of the trip.
options.bring: High altitude: go slowly and rest when you need to. The sun is strong and the weather changes quickly: layers and a rain jacket.
options.accessibility: Flat ground on cobbled streets, no steps, at 3,400 m. Wheelchairs can follow the route but cobbles are uneven and the air is thin.

options.name: Sacred Valley: Chinchero
options.difficulty_note: About 3 km of walking on uneven ground and Inca stone steps, at around 3,800 m. Some short climbs. The weaving demonstration is seated.
options.description: Today we climb into the Andean sky to Chinchero, a weaver's village older than the Inca. Women in bright shawls show us how wool is dyed with plants, crushed insects and flowers, then spun and woven by hand. We walk the terraces the Inca built, step into a church painted by candlelight, and leave with the feeling of having been welcomed into a living tradition.
options.bring: High altitude: go slowly and rest when you need to. The sun is strong and the weather changes quickly: layers and a rain jacket.
options.accessibility: Some steps or uneven ground. Guests with limited mobility should speak to their guide before choosing this tour.

options.name: Maras and Moray
options.difficulty_note: About 2 km of walking in total, with steps down into the Moray terraces (optional) and uneven paths at the salt pans, at around 3,500 m.
options.description: Today we visit two places that look like they came from another world. At Moray, circular terraces sink into the earth like a giant amphitheatre, perhaps the Inca's open-air laboratory. At Maras, thousands of shimmering salt pools still glitter on the mountainside, worked by families for centuries. Bring your camera; the light here is extraordinary.
options.bring: High altitude: go slowly and rest when you need to. The sun is strong and the weather changes quickly: layers and a rain jacket.
options.accessibility: Some steps or uneven ground. Guests with limited mobility should speak to their guide before choosing this tour.

options.name: Cusco City Tour
options.difficulty_note: Short walks on cobbled streets with a few steps, at 3,400 m. Frequent stops. Coach between sites.
options.description: Today we walk through the heart of the Inca empire. On the Plaza de Armas we learn how a capital shaped like a puma became a Spanish city, and at the Coricancha, once plated in gold, we see Inca stonework so precise that no blade fits between the blocks. The story of two worlds colliding is written in these walls.
options.bring: High altitude: go slowly and rest when you need to. The sun is strong and the weather changes quickly: layers and a rain jacket.
options.accessibility: The cathedral and the Coricancha are step-free at the entrances, with a few steps inside. The Plaza de Armas is flat but cobbled. Several uneven stone floors.

options.name: Sacsayhuaman
options.difficulty_note: About 2 km on grass and uneven stone at 3,700 m, with a climb of about 100 m. Slow pace.
options.description: Today we stand beneath the walls of Sacsayhuaman, a fortress built with stones that weigh as much as a lorry, fitted together without mortar. Our guide tells how it was built, how it fell, and why Cusco still looks up to it. From the top, the whole red-roofed city lies at our feet.
options.bring: High altitude: go slowly and rest when you need to. The sun is strong and the weather changes quickly: layers and a rain jacket.
options.accessibility: The site is on a slope, with grass and stone steps up to the platform and no lift. Not suitable for wheelchairs.

options.name: Machu Picchu by train
options.difficulty_note: A train ride, a bus up the mountain, then about 3 km of walking with many stone steps on the citadel, at 2,400 m. Long day. A guide can set a slower pace.
options.description: Today we board the scenic train that follows the roaring Urubamba river into the cloud forest, and then, at last, we climb to the lost city of the Incas. Machu Picchu appears out of the mist, terraces draped over the mountain, and our guide leads us through temples and royal rooms. It is the day many of us have dreamed about for years.
options.bring: High altitude: go slowly and rest when you need to. The sun is strong and the weather changes quickly: layers and a rain jacket.
options.accessibility: The train has level boarding with a step; luggage racks are narrow. Inside the site there are about 250 stone steps up to the main viewpoints and no handrails in places. Not suitable for wheelchairs.

options.name: Ahu Tahai at sunset
options.difficulty_note: Flat, short walk on grass. Windy.
options.description: Today we meet the moai at the best hour of the day. As the sun sinks into the Pacific, the restored statues of Ahu Tahai glow gold, and a local Rapa Nui guide tells the story of the people who carved them and carried them across the island. There is nothing between you and the horizon. Stay for the last light.
options.bring: Very windy and exposed: a windproof jacket. Do not climb on or touch the statues or the platforms.
options.accessibility: Mostly level and gentle: suitable for most guests, including those who walk slowly. Tell your guide if you use a wheelchair or a walker and we will check access for you.

options.name: Rano Raraku and Ahu Tongariki
options.difficulty_note: About 3 km on grass and uneven volcanic ground, with a climb of about 60 m at the quarry. Little shade, strong sun and wind.
options.description: Today we walk into the quarry where the moai were born. Nearly 400 statues, some finished, some half-carved, stare out from the slopes of Rano Raraku as if the sculptors had just put down their tools. Then, at Ahu Tongariki, fifteen giants stand in a row facing the sea. It is one of the most powerful sights on Earth.
options.bring: Very windy and exposed: a windproof jacket. Do not climb on or touch the statues or the platforms.
options.accessibility: Some steps or uneven ground. Guests with limited mobility should speak to their guide before choosing this tour.

options.name: Anakena beach and Ahu Nau Nau
options.difficulty_note: Flat, soft sand. Swimming is optional.
options.description: Today we visit the one white-sand beach on Easter Island, the place where, legend says, the first king landed. Palm trees sway behind the moai of Ahu Nau Nau, the best-preserved on the island, some still wearing their red topknots. Swim, walk, and imagine the canoes arriving a thousand years ago.
options.bring: The sun is strong: hat and sun cream. Swimwear and a towel if you want to swim.
options.accessibility: Mostly level and gentle: suitable for most guests, including those who walk slowly. Tell your guide if you use a wheelchair or a walker and we will check access for you.

options.name: Orongo ceremonial village
options.difficulty_note: A drive to the crater rim, then about 1 km on a flat path. Strong wind; keep to the path near the edge.
options.description: Today we stand on the rim of a crater, 300 metres above the sea, where young men once raced to bring back the first egg of the sooty tern. Among the stone houses of Orongo, petroglyphs of the birdman look out over the islets, and the wind tells the story. The view alone is worth the journey.
options.bring: Very windy and exposed: a windproof jacket. Do not climb on or touch the statues or the platforms.
options.accessibility: Mostly level and gentle: suitable for most guests, including those who walk slowly. Tell your guide if you use a wheelchair or a walker and we will check access for you.

options.name: Welcome kava ceremony
options.difficulty_note: Seated, on mats on the floor (a chair is available).
options.description: Today a Samoan chief welcomes us the way travellers have been welcomed here for centuries. We sit in a circle, the kava is prepared and passed in a coconut cup, songs rise in the air, and we learn what fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, truly means. This is not a show. It is an invitation.
options.bring: Smart casual.
options.accessibility: We sit on mats on the floor in a traditional open house. A chair can be provided. One step at the entrance.

options.name: Vailima
options.difficulty_note: A gentle climb of about 40 steps to the house and a flat garden. Hot and humid.
options.description: Today we walk in the footsteps of Robert Louis Stevenson. The author of Treasure Island left Scotland, searching for a place to breathe, and found it on this green hillside above Apia, where the Samoans called him Tusitala, the teller of tales. We tour his house, stroll through the garden he loved, and, if we wish, climb to the hilltop where he chose to be buried, looking out over the Pacific.
options.bring: Hot, humid, and it may rain: a light rain jacket and insect repellent. Stay on the paths.
options.accessibility: The museum is a two-floor house with no lift: the first floor is reached by a flight of about 40 steps with a handrail. The garden is level. The walk to the tomb is optional and takes about 45 minutes uphill on a steep path.

options.name: Women's Committee
options.difficulty_note: Seated on mats for part of the visit (chairs available). Flat ground. Hot and humid.
options.description: Today we are invited into the heart of a Samoan village. The women's committee, which runs the health and daily life of the community, shows us how bark cloth is pounded and painted, how pandanus leaves become fine mats, and how a village takes care of its own. Sit, listen, and perhaps try your hand at weaving.
options.bring: Closed shoes in the kitchen. Tell your guide about any allergy.
options.accessibility: Seating is on mats on the floor; chairs are available on request. The meeting house is one level with a single step at the entrance.

options.name: Lalomanu beach
options.difficulty_note: Flat sand. Swimming is optional. A shaded beach fale is booked for the group.
options.description: Today is for the postcard. A long ribbon of white sand, water in four shades of blue, and fale huts under the palms. Swim, snorkel straight from the shore, and then share a barbecue under the trees with the whole group. Nothing to see. Just everything to feel.
options.bring: The sun is strong: hat and sun cream. Swimwear and a towel if you want to swim.
options.accessibility: Soft sand and a few steps down to the beach. Tables under the trees are on sand. Not suitable for wheelchairs.

options.name: Great Barrier Reef
options.difficulty_note: About 1.5 hours each way by catamaran, which can be rough. About 2 hours in the water, snorkelling in a life vest or with a noodle. You must be comfortable in open water.
options.description: Today we sail out to the largest living structure on the planet. By catamaran we reach the outer reef, and a marine biologist introduces us to the coral gardens we are about to drift over. Turtles glide past, fish flash in every colour, and lunch is served on deck. You will remember this water for the rest of your life.
options.bring: Swimsuit and a towel. Reef-safe sun cream only. Touching the coral is not allowed.
options.accessibility: You step on and off the catamaran from a pontoon, with crew help, and a ladder or platform to enter the water. Floating aids are provided. Lifts: none. Please tell your leader about any health condition before choosing.

options.name: Daintree Rainforest
options.difficulty_note: About 2 km on boardwalks and gravel paths, hot and humid. A river cruise is seated.
options.description: Today we step into the oldest rainforest on Earth, 180 million years old, older than the Amazon. We glide down a river with our eyes on the banks for crocodiles, then walk a boardwalk through ferns the size of trees, listening for cassowaries. Every sound here is ancient.
options.bring: Hot, humid, and it may rain: a light rain jacket and insect repellent. Stay on the paths.
options.accessibility: The river boat has two steps to board and fixed seats. The boardwalk is flat and wide, about 800 m, with a few ramps and no steps. A wheelchair can use the boardwalk.

options.name: Old Market and Apsara dance
options.difficulty_note: A short, flat walk in a busy market. Hot.
options.description: Today Siem Reap shows us its senses. We wander the Old Market with a local guide, tasting, smelling and bargaining, and in the evening we sit in a candlelit courtyard to watch Apsara dancers, whose gestures have been passed down from the walls of Angkor itself. It is a feast for the eyes.
options.bring: Crowded and busy: keep valuables close. Covered shoulders and knees are appreciated. Ask before photographing people.
options.accessibility: Mostly level and gentle: suitable for most guests, including those who walk slowly. Tell your guide if you use a wheelchair or a walker and we will check access for you.

options.name: Angkor Wat, Ta Prohm, and Angkor Thom
options.difficulty_note: About 4 km of walking on stone, with steep, narrow steps at Angkor Wat (a lower route is available). Very hot from mid-morning. Start is early on purpose.
options.description: Today we explore three wonders of the world in a single day. Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument on Earth, rises from its moat; at Angkor Thom the stone faces of the Bayon smile at us from every tower; and at Ta Prohm, giant tree roots swallow the temple whole. Arrive early. The morning light is magic.
options.bring: Cover shoulders and knees: these are religious sites. Early start; the sun is strong from mid-morning.
options.accessibility: Angkor Wat has steep stone steps to the upper level (optional, about 70 steps with handrails). Ta Prohm has uneven ground and wooden walkways. Angkor Thom is mostly flat. Not suitable for wheelchairs.

options.name: Beng Mealea
options.difficulty_note: About 2 km clambering over fallen stones on wooden walkways and uneven ground. A 1 hour 15 minute drive each way. Hot.
options.description: Today we play explorers. Beng Mealea is a vast temple that the jungle has been reclaiming for centuries, and we climb over fallen towers, duck through half-collapsed galleries and follow moss-covered corridors where almost no one else goes. It feels like discovering the temple for the first time.
options.bring: Cover shoulders and knees: these are religious sites. Early start; the sun is strong from mid-morning.
options.accessibility: Rubble, fallen stones and slippery moss: walking is uneven throughout and climbing is part of the visit. Not suitable for wheelchairs or walking aids.

options.name: Roluos Temple Complex
options.difficulty_note: Short, flat walks between three sites, with a few steps at each. Hot.
options.description: Today we travel back to where Angkor began. The temples of Roluos, Preah Ko, Bakong and Lolei, were built more than a thousand years ago, long before Angkor Wat, and their brick towers and delicate carvings tell the story of the first Khmer capital. Quiet, beautiful, and almost ours alone.
options.bring: Cover shoulders and knees: these are religious sites. Early start; the sun is strong from mid-morning.
options.accessibility: Short walks on grass and gravel, with a few steep stone steps at each temple (optional). Partly accessible.

options.name: Private Cooking Lesson
options.difficulty_note: Standing at a cooking table, indoors. Flat. Light physical effort.
options.description: Today we cook like a Cambodian family. We pick herbs in a garden, learn the secrets of fresh amok and sour soups from a local chef, and then sit down to eat what we have made. You will leave with a recipe, a full stomach, and a story to retell at home.
options.bring: Closed shoes in the kitchen. Tell your guide about any allergy.
options.accessibility: A covered, open-sided kitchen on level ground. Cooking is done standing or seated on a stool. Suitable for most guests.

options.name: APOPO HeroRATs Visitor Center
options.difficulty_note: Indoors and short flat walks. Light.
options.description: Today we meet the smallest heroes of Cambodia: giant pouched rats trained to sniff out landmines that still lie beneath the soil. We see how they work, meet the people who train them, and learn how every cleared field becomes a school, a farm or a home. It is a story that will stay with you.
options.bring: Comfortable closed shoes. A sun hat in summer.
options.accessibility: One level, ramps at the entrance, and a flat path to the demonstration area. Step-free and suitable for wheelchairs.

options.name: Angkor Wat, Ta Prohm, and Angkor Thom
options.difficulty_note: About 4 km of walking on stone, with steep, narrow steps at Angkor Wat (a lower route is available). Very hot from mid-morning. Start is early on purpose.
options.description: Today we explore three wonders of the world in a single day. Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument on Earth, rises from its moat; at Angkor Thom the stone faces of the Bayon smile at us from every tower; and at Ta Prohm, giant tree roots swallow the temple whole. Arrive early. The morning light is magic.
options.bring: Cover shoulders and knees: these are religious sites. Early start; the sun is strong from mid-morning.
options.accessibility: Angkor Wat has steep stone steps to the upper level (optional, about 70 steps with handrails). Ta Prohm has uneven ground and wooden walkways. Angkor Thom is mostly flat. Not suitable for wheelchairs.

options.name: Beng Mealea
options.difficulty_note: About 2 km clambering over fallen stones on wooden walkways and uneven ground. A 1 hour 15 minute drive each way. Hot.
options.description: Today we play explorers. Beng Mealea is a vast temple that the jungle has been reclaiming for centuries, and we climb over fallen towers, duck through half-collapsed galleries and follow moss-covered corridors where almost no one else goes. It feels like discovering the temple for the first time.
options.bring: Cover shoulders and knees: these are religious sites. Early start; the sun is strong from mid-morning.
options.accessibility: Rubble, fallen stones and slippery moss: walking is uneven throughout and climbing is part of the visit. Not suitable for wheelchairs or walking aids.

options.name: Roluos Temple Complex
options.difficulty_note: Short, flat walks between three sites, with a few steps at each. Hot.
options.description: Today we travel back to where Angkor began. The temples of Roluos, Preah Ko, Bakong and Lolei, were built more than a thousand years ago, long before Angkor Wat, and their brick towers and delicate carvings tell the story of the first Khmer capital. Quiet, beautiful, and almost ours alone.
options.bring: Cover shoulders and knees: these are religious sites. Early start; the sun is strong from mid-morning.
options.accessibility: Short walks on grass and gravel, with a few steep stone steps at each temple (optional). Partly accessible.

options.name: Private Cooking Lesson
options.difficulty_note: Standing at a cooking table, indoors. Flat. Light physical effort.
options.description: Today we cook like a Cambodian family. We pick herbs in a garden, learn the secrets of fresh amok and sour soups from a local chef, and then sit down to eat what we have made. You will leave with a recipe, a full stomach, and a story to retell at home.
options.bring: Closed shoes in the kitchen. Tell your guide about any allergy.
options.accessibility: A covered, open-sided kitchen on level ground. Cooking is done standing or seated on a stool. Suitable for most guests.

options.name: APOPO HeroRATs Visitor Center
options.difficulty_note: Indoors and short flat walks. Light.
options.description: Today we meet the smallest heroes of Cambodia: giant pouched rats trained to sniff out landmines that still lie beneath the soil. We see how they work, meet the people who train them, and learn how every cleared field becomes a school, a farm or a home. It is a story that will stay with you.
options.bring: Comfortable closed shoes. A sun hat in summer.
options.accessibility: One level, ramps at the entrance, and a flat path to the demonstration area. Step-free and suitable for wheelchairs.

options.name: Durbar Square walk
options.difficulty_note: About 2 km on uneven brick paving with a few steps, among crowds and traffic.
options.description: Today we walk through the beating heart of old Kathmandu. Around the royal square, carved wooden temples crowd together, pigeons rise in clouds, and in a small window the Kumari, the living goddess, may appear. Our guide helps us read a city where gods and everyday life share the same streets.
options.bring: Cover shoulders and knees, and walk clockwise around the stupa. Photography is not allowed in some places: your guide will say where.
options.accessibility: Flat paving in the square, but the temples stand on tall stepped plinths (up to 8 steps) and none have lifts. Narrow lanes and cycle rickshaws. Partly accessible.

options.name: Boudhanath and Pashupatinath
options.difficulty_note: About 3 km on foot over uneven ground and many steps at Pashupatinath. Crowded. The cremation ghats at Pashupatinath may be upsetting for some people; photography is limited.
options.description: Today we meet two sacred places that no one forgets. At Boudhanath, we walk clockwise around one of the biggest stupas in the world, among pilgrims, butter lamps and fluttering prayer flags. At Pashupatinath, on the banks of the Bagmati river, we watch a Hindu temple complex alive with devotion. Open hearts, quiet voices.
options.bring: Cover shoulders and knees, and walk clockwise around the stupa. Photography is not allowed in some places: your guide will say where.
options.accessibility: The Boudhanath circuit is flat but crowded and paved with worn stones. Pashupatinath has long stairways with no handrails. Partly accessible.

options.name: Thimphu
options.difficulty_note: About 1 hour 30 minutes by coach each way on a winding road. Short, flat walks in the capital. Some people feel carsick on the bends.
options.description: Today we visit the only capital in the world without a single traffic light. In Thimphu, a giant golden Buddha looks out over the valley, a folk heritage museum shows how Bhutanese farm families lived, and the paper-making workshop turns bark into art. A small kingdom with a very big soul.
options.bring: Cover shoulders and knees. No photographs inside the monastery, and bags are left at the entrance. A warm layer: it is cold at height.
options.accessibility: The Buddha viewing platform is reached by about 20 steps, with a ramp on one side. The heritage museum is a three-floor traditional house with steep wooden stairs and no lift.

options.name: Tiger's Nest Hike
options.difficulty_note: About 10 km round trip with a climb of roughly 900 m, starting at 2,600 m above sea level, so the air is thin. Around 700 uneven steps near the top. Allow 4 hours up and 2 hours down. Not recommended with heart or knee problems or a fear of heights: some stretches are narrow with a drop beside the path. Horses can carry you part of the way up.
options.description: Today we climb to one of the most breathtaking temples ever built. Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest, clings to a cliff 900 metres above the Paro valley, and we reach it on foot through pine forests, prayer flags and a stairway cut into the rock. Hard work. Unforgettable reward. A teahouse waits halfway.
options.bring: Cover shoulders and knees. No photographs inside the monastery, and bags are left at the entrance. A warm layer: it is cold at height.
options.accessibility: A climb of about 800 m of height over roughly 3 to 4 hours, with some 700 steps near the top and no handrails in places. A pony can help for the first part (extra cost). Not suitable for wheelchairs or for guests with heart or knee problems.

options.name: Agra Fort and Mehtab Bagh sunset
options.difficulty_note: About 1.5 km on flat and slightly sloping stone at the fort. Hot and dusty.
options.description: Today we follow the Mughal emperors. In the red sandstone fort of Agra, we walk the rooms where Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal, was held prisoner, looking out at the monument he loved. Then, in a quiet garden across the river, we wait as the Taj turns from white to gold to pink. It is pure magic.
options.bring: Shoes are removed or covered on the marble. Large bags and tripods are not allowed. Cover shoulders and knees.
options.accessibility: The fort has ramps that are steep and paved with old stone, and some stairs without handrails. The garden is flat and grassy. Partly accessible.

options.name: Taj Mahal at sunrise
options.difficulty_note: About 1.5 km on flat marble and paths. Early start. Shoe covers or bare feet on the marble.
options.description: Today we rise before dawn to meet the world's greatest love story. As the first light touches the marble, the Taj Mahal changes from grey to pearl to rose, and our guide tells of the emperor who built it for his wife. The crowds are small. The silence is huge. This is the moment of the whole trip.
options.bring: Shoes are removed or covered on the marble. Large bags and tripods are not allowed. Cover shoulders and knees.
options.accessibility: The approach is flat, about 600 m from the gate, with 8 steps to the marble platform and a ramp on one side. Shoe covers are provided. Wheelchairs can be used with help.

options.name: Marble inlay workshop
options.difficulty_note: Seated indoors. No walking.
options.description: Today we step into a family workshop where the same craft that decorated the Taj Mahal is still practised. Craftsmen cut tiny pieces of semi-precious stones, shape them by hand and set them into marble with patience that seems to stop time. Watch, ask, and take home a piece of the story.
options.bring: Ask before touching the work. Photography may not be allowed in some workshops.
options.accessibility: A ground-floor workshop with one step at the door. The showroom upstairs is optional and has no lift.

options.name: First game drive
options.difficulty_note: Seated in an open safari vehicle on rough tracks: bumpy, with dust. Getting in and out needs a step.
options.description: Today the Serengeti opens. With a ranger who reads the plains like a book, we drive out into the golden grass, searching for lions in the shade, elephants at the waterhole and giraffes against the sky. Everything is wild, and everything is close. Keep your eyes open and your camera ready.
options.bring: Open vehicle: dust, sun, and cold at dawn. Layers, a hat, neutral colours. Stay seated and quiet near the animals.
options.accessibility: The vehicle has a high step (a stool is provided) and a roof that opens. Seats are fixed and the ride is bumpy. Tell your leader if you use a wheelchair: not every vehicle can carry one.

options.name: Serengeti game drive
options.difficulty_note: Seated in an open vehicle on rough tracks for most of the day. Bumpy, hot and dusty. Picnic lunch in the bush.
options.description: Today we give ourselves a whole day on the plains. We track the great herds with a picnic lunch under an acacia, stop at a hippo pool to watch the grunting giants, and climb a rocky outcrop for a view that goes on forever. This is the Africa you saw in documentaries, and now you are in it.
options.bring: Open vehicle: dust, sun, and cold at dawn. Layers, a hat, neutral colours. Stay seated and quiet near the animals.
options.accessibility: The vehicle has a high step (a stool is provided) and the ride is bumpy over a full day. Toilets are basic bush stops. Tell your leader if you use a wheelchair.

options.name: Ngorongoro Crater Safari
options.difficulty_note: A long drive each way on rough tracks, including a steep descent of about 600 m into the crater by 4x4. Cold at dawn, hot at midday.
options.description: Today we descend into a lost world. The Ngorongoro Crater, the largest intact volcanic caldera on Earth, holds lions, rhinos, hippos, flamingos and thousands of grazers in a single green bowl. We drive down at first light, and by lunchtime we have seen more wildlife than many people see in a lifetime.
options.bring: Very windy and exposed: a windproof jacket. Do not climb on or touch the statues or the platforms.
options.accessibility: The road down the crater wall is steep and winding, and the vehicle step is high (a stool is provided). The drive is long and bumpy. Tell your leader about back problems.

options.name: Olduvai Gorge
options.difficulty_note: A long drive on rough roads and a short walk at the gorge. Seated for the talk in the museum.
options.description: Today we stand in the cradle of humankind. In this dry gorge, scientists found some of the oldest remains of our ancestors, and our guide tells how bones, tools and footprints rewrote the story of who we are. A small museum, a vast idea. You will look at your own hands differently afterwards.
options.bring: Open vehicle: dust, sun, and cold at dawn. Layers, a hat, neutral colours. Stay seated and quiet near the animals.
options.accessibility: The small museum is on one level with a ramp. The gorge viewpoint is a short walk on flat ground.

options.name: Sunrise game drive
options.difficulty_note: Seated in an open vehicle, cold at first light. Bumpy.
options.description: Today we say goodbye to the Serengeti the best way possible: in the first light, when the animals are most active. The grass glows, a hot drink steams in our hands, and the plains slowly wake around us. A last drive, a last lion, and a memory to keep.
options.bring: Open vehicle: dust, sun, and cold at dawn. Layers, a hat, neutral colours. Stay seated and quiet near the animals.
options.accessibility: The vehicle has a high step (a stool is provided), and it is cold in the open air at dawn. The ride is bumpy.

options.name: Little Petra
options.difficulty_note: A short drive and about 1 km of gentle walking on sand and rock steps.
options.description: Today we discover Petra's quieter sister. Siq al-Barid, Little Petra, is a narrow canyon of carved dwellings and dining rooms where Nabataean traders once rested, and we climb a rock stairway to a painted ceiling that still holds its colours. Afterwards, a Bedouin family serves us tea in the shade. Peaceful and unforgettable.
options.bring: The sun is strong and there is little shade: hat and sturdy closed shoes. Keep to the paths and do not climb on the monuments.
options.accessibility: The canyon floor is flat, but the climb to the painted ceiling is a rock stairway of about 40 steps without handrails (optional). Partly accessible.

options.name: Petra by Night
options.difficulty_note: About 3 km on sand and uneven stone in the dark, along the 1.2 km Siq to the Treasury and back. A torch is provided. Cool at night.
options.description: Today we walk into a story told by candlelight. The Siq, the narrow canyon that leads to Petra, glows with thousands of candles, and at the end, the Treasury appears out of the dark. We sit on the ground, hear a Bedouin musician play, and drink sweet tea under the stars. Few experiences are so quiet and so magical.
options.bring: The sun is strong and there is little shade: hat and sturdy closed shoes. Keep to the paths and do not climb on the monuments.
options.accessibility: The Siq is 1.2 km on uneven sandy paving, walked in the dark by candlelight. Seating at the Treasury is on mats on the ground. Not suitable for wheelchairs. A horse or cart is available for part of the way.

options.name: Petra Siq and Treasury
options.difficulty_note: About 8 km on sand and stone with some steps. A horse ride is possible for the first 800 m. Very hot from late morning. Long day.
options.description: Today we enter the rose-red city. We walk the 1.2 km Siq, a canyon where the walls close in and the sky narrows, until a gap opens and the Treasury appears, carved into the cliff. Beyond it lie the Street of Facades, the Theatre and the Royal Tombs. This is the moment the whole trip leads to.
options.bring: The sun is strong and there is little shade: hat and sturdy closed shoes. Keep to the paths and do not climb on the monuments.
options.accessibility: The Siq is 1.2 km of uneven paving with a gentle slope, and the Street of Facades is longer. Horse carts take you to the Treasury (extra cost). Partly accessible with help.

options.name: High Place of Sacrifice
options.difficulty_note: A climb of about 200 m by 600 rock steps, in the heat, with exposed sections and no handrails. Good fitness and a head for heights are needed.
options.description: Today we climb as the Nabataeans did. A stone stairway carved into the mountain leads to a sacred platform high above Petra, and from the top, the entire rose-red valley stretches out below us. It is a hard climb and a perfect reward. Few visitors come this way.
options.bring: The sun is strong and there is little shade: hat and sturdy closed shoes. Keep to the paths and do not climb on the monuments.
options.accessibility: A climb of roughly 800 rock-cut steps, uneven and without handrails, over 2 hours. Not suitable for wheelchairs, or for guests with heart, knee or balance problems.

options.name: Marrakech City Tour
options.difficulty_note: About 4 km of easy walking with breaks, on flat stone streets and in crowded souks. Hot in the afternoon.
options.description: Today we plunge into the red city. We climb the Koutoubia minaret's shadow, wander the painted halls of the Bahia Palace, stand in the silent Saadian Tombs and then dive into the Jemaa el-Fna square, where snake charmers, storytellers and food stalls make a show of everyday life. Marrakech wakes all your senses at once.
options.bring: Crowded and busy: keep valuables close. Covered shoulders and knees are appreciated. Ask before photographing people.
options.accessibility: The Bahia Palace has uneven tiled floors and low doorways, the Saadian Tombs are on one level with a step, and the souks are crowded and cobbled. Mostly step-free but not easy by wheelchair.

options.name: Atlas Mountains Hike
options.difficulty_note: About 8 km of walking on mountain paths with a climb of roughly 400 m, at up to 1,800 m. A 1 hour drive each way. Rocky ground, some stream crossings.
options.description: Today we leave the city for the high Atlas. With a mountain guide, we walk through a Berber valley of terraced fields and walnut trees, cross a stream and stop in a village where a family invites us for mint tea and fresh bread. Quiet paths, snow-capped peaks, warm hospitality.
options.bring: Mountain weather changes fast: layers and sturdy shoes. The sun is strong at height.
options.accessibility: Paths are uneven, with stone steps and a stream crossing on stepping stones. Walking poles are available. Not suitable for wheelchairs.

options.name: Moroccan Culinary Tour
options.difficulty_note: About 2 km of walking in total, in crowded lanes. Standing at a cooking table for part of the day.
options.description: Today we taste Marrakech like locals. We wander the souks, choosing spices, olives and vegetables with a chef, and then, in the kitchen of a riad, we cook a tagine and a pastilla, learning every secret. You will eat what you cooked, and you will never forget the smell of the spice stalls.
options.bring: Closed shoes in the kitchen. Tell your guide about any allergy.
options.accessibility: A walk in crowded souks, then a riad kitchen with a few steps up from the courtyard. The riad has no lift.

options.name: Farewell brunch
options.difficulty_note: Seated. No walking.
options.description: Today we end the journey the way it deserves. A long, slow brunch in a garden, with the whole group and the expedition team, and plenty of time to share the moments that mattered most. Twenty-five days, twelve countries, one table. Raise a glass.
options.bring: Smart casual.
options.accessibility: A garden on one level with gravel paths. Tables and chairs on flat ground. Step-free.
